title: Console live trace lab - Lakemount Retail
summary: Redwood ran a focused console walkthrough showing trace visualization, request playback, and error analysis for Lakemount Retail's inference pipelines. Discussed KV cache behavior, fallback policies, VPC deployment constraints, and quantitative benchmarks needed for a pilot. Agreed next steps: Redwood to run a short replay on sample traces, share security docs and cost/throughput sketch, and schedule a 1-week pilot kickoff (POC).
topics: Console trace map and hop visualization
KV cache and prefix caching behavior
action_items: Ethan (Redwood SE): run replay of 3 anonymized failing traces and share logs - due 2026-09-29
Maya (AE): send pilot pricing sketch and security whitepaper (SOC2 summary + KMS integration doc) - due 2026-09-24
Sofia (Lakemount): provide 3 example request IDs and sample payloads (sanitized) - due 2026-09-25
next_steps: Redwood to run trace replay and return artifacts (playback recordings + console links)
Schedule pilot kickoff for week of 2026-09-29
Lakemount to confirm compliance checklist items and provide sample traffic profile
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-09-22 17:30 PDT / Duration ~52 minutes. Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Zhang (Redwood SE), Sofia Reyes (Lakemount - Director ML), Tom Nguyen (Platform Eng), Priya Sharma (SRE).

Summary (auto): Quick console lab — trace map, request inspector, error playback, and discussion of VPC/KMS concerns.

[00:00] Maya (Redwood): hey everyone thanks for joining, can you hear me ok?
[00:04] Sofia (Lakemount): yep can hear you, thanks Maya. We got a full team today, Tom and Priya are on to talk infra stuff.
[00:10] Maya: perfect, i'll do a 3-4 minute context pull then ethan will jump into the console and we will walk through a couple of real traces you shared. sound good?
[00:18] Tom (Lakemount): yep sounds good.
[00:20] Ethan (Redwood): cool, quick heads up i'll be demoing from the staging console, not production, so some links will be placeholders. also apologies in advance, i tend to talk fast when i'm excited.
[00:29] Priya: that's fine.

[00:31] Maya: so high level we know you run a mix of in-house models for personalization and a small number of third-party models. you're seeing occasional timeouts and higher tail latency during peak checkout flows, and some 500-style errors that are hard to reproduce from logs. goal today is to show console tracing and request playback to make reproduction and root cause analysis easier. correct?
[00:48] Sofia: yep, that's the gist. we also want to understand if the Redwood runtime would give us predictable latencies without blowing budget — and if we go private/VPC how much changes.
[00:58] Maya: great. ethan, take it away.

[01:02] [01:02] Ethan: okay i'm in the console, opening the trace map for the last 24 hours. you can see on the left we have a timeline and an aggregated heatmap of hotspots. here is a cluster of requests with elevated p95 — looks like around 17:12 UTC. i'll zoom into that window.
[01:20] Sofia: can you show the request ids? we sent a list yesterday but not sure if they fall in that window.
[01:25] Ethan: yeah, i'm filtering by those IDs now — ok there they are. selecting a single request. this is the trace view: call graph shows the frontend gateway, routing layer, then inference runtime pod. note the hop map — the orange segment here indicates KV cache miss and a fallback to full context decode.
[01:45] Tom: hm KV cache miss — we saw some of that in our logs but didn't realize it caused full context re-decode, thought it was only partial.
[01:52] Ethan: common confusion — our trace annotates cache hits vs misses; a miss can mean either empty prefix cache or incompatible key (e.g., model variant or sequence length mismatch). console labels the exact reason when available, but sometimes the telemetry pipeline infers it which can be fuzzy — hence the transcription: 'cue vee cache' in older exports.
[02:10] Priya: that's helpful. can the console replay the exact request with original KV state?
[02:15] Ethan: yes, request playback can be done two ways — a deterministic replay that rehydrates the KV and runs on an identical model snapshot (if you pin model version), or a best-effort replay that uses current live routing and will record deviations. for debugging we recommend deterministic where possible.
[02:34] Sofia: do you need our KMS keys to do deterministic replay if we're on VPC?
[02:39] Ethan: good question — for private deployments we don't store customer KMS keys in Redwood; we integrate with your KMS via key wrap and access delegation. for running a replay in your VPC you would either run the playback job inside the VPC (preferred) or redact sensitive payloads and let us replay in staging. we'll add this to the security notes.
[02:58] Maya: quick check — latency SLOs you're targeting was 200ms p95 on the personalization path?
[03:04] Sofia: ideally yes, 200ms p95, <50ms median if possible but the p95 is the hard one.
[03:09] Maya: okay we'll show the p95 view and then talk about batching trade-offs. ethan, continue.

[03:14] [03:14] Ethan: jumping to request inspector — you can see token-level timing and per-kernel breakdown. there's a big spike in the first chunk of tokens — that corresponds to a quantize-decode path where we hit a software kernel that isn't fusable on this GPU. console suggests a quantization profile change; notice the annotation here: 'suggested qprofile: int8-symmetric-v2 for shorter sequences'.
[03:36] Tom: we currently run int8 with a homegrown quant config, does Redwood support custom kernel overrides?
[03:42] Ethan: yes you can provide a custom compilation flag and we can register a kernel override in Dedicated deployments. in Hosted we expose curated qprofiles; in Private you get full control. caveat — custom kernels affect rollouts so we recommend A/Bing on a small percentage.
[03:56] Priya: about rollbacks — if a rollout causes errors, will the traffic automatically fallback to a previous model?
[04:02] Ethan: yes, we have automatic fallback policies. console shows an active policy: fallback to 'smaller-llama-13b-q4' on >5% error rate in a 5m window. you can tune thresholds per-route.
[04:13] Sofia: nice. and the console shows that history?
[04:16] Ethan: yep, playback and trace map will show points where fallback occurred and which requests were served by fallback. here's an example trace where the runtime shifted to fallback at token 12. you can expand the trace to see exact decision log.

[04:30] [04:30] Maya: can we flip to multi-request batching behavior — they mentioned that high concurrency causes latency tail when shapes vary.
[04:36] Ethan: sure. switching to Batching Insights. you can see batch size distribution and sequence length histogram. when we have mixed short and long sequences, the runtime may wait a small micro-batch to fill tokens which improves throughput but hurts tail latency. console has suggestions: shape-aware batching and a per-route max-wait of 8ms for latency sensitive flows.
[04:56] Tom: can we configure shape-aware batching on dedicated pools?
[04:59] Ethan: yes, it's a runtime config on Dedicated and Private. Hosted exposes shape-aware heuristics but not per-customer tuning.
[05:06] Sofia: quick Q — what about our internal observability? do we get token-level logs off the console?
[05:11] Ethan: yes, you can export token-timeline traces to your SIEM or S3; we also support sending structured events to Datadog and Splunk. note that token timelines can be large so we have sampling and redaction controls.

[05:26] [05:26] Priya: one more infra-level — when you say 'route by policy' can we pin a route to run only in us-east-1 GPUs? we need data residency for EU stuff.
[05:33] Ethan: you can pin by region, instance type, or capacity tier. for EU residency we'd deploy a private plane in the EU region or run Dedicated nodes in eu-west, and you can pin the route. console shows active region routing and fallbacks.
[05:45] Sofia: what about audit logs and SSO/SAML?
[05:48] Maya: we support SSO with SAML, RBAC with granular roles, and audit events for request acceptance and model pulls. security whitepaper covers retention windows and who can see token-level traces.
[05:59] Tom: will the redacted transcripts still be useful for debugging? sometimes redaction hides the error signal.
[06:04] Ethan: yeah it's a balance — console can keep a redaction toggle per-playback job. for PII we recommend keeping a hashed fingerprint of sensitive fields so you can still correlate without revealing text.

[06:20] [06:20] Ethan: ok i'm going to run a live playback of one of the sample traces you gave — i'll run it deterministically against a pinned snapshot. starting playback now — recording the session.
[06:30] Sofia: curious to see if we repro the timing anomaly.
[06:33] [06:33] (audio: brief typing and console noise)
[06:45] Ethan: running — it's replaying the original token stream. you'll see timings on the left. ah yep — see that spike at token 6 — that's the same shape as your production trace. the console shows the kernel fallback here; in the log panel it says 'cuBLAS kernel timeout, falling back to CPU kernel'.
[07:04] Priya: cuBLAS timeout — is that from driver or from overloaded GPU?
[07:09] Ethan: usually it means the GPU kernel attempted a long-running op and hit a watchdog, but it can be noisy — also driver mismatch or a bad kernel selection. we can correlate with GPU metrics; console links to the node metrics panel.
[07:21] Tom: would moving to a different GPU family help? we run older A100s on prem.
[07:26] Ethan: possibly — newer Ampere or Blackwell variants have better kernel fusion support. also compilation flags can produce less aggressive kernels that avoid timeout at the cost of some throughput.

[07:38] [07:38] Sofia: about costs — if we patch quantization to avoid the fallback, do we have concrete per-token cost delta?
[07:45] Maya: we can produce a sketch — typically avoiding a CPU fallback reduces per-token cost by 3-6x in the affected path, because CPU decode is much slower. we'll include numbers in the pricing sketch.
[07:56] Sofia: good.

[07:58] [07:58] Ethan: ok i'm pausing playback. next, i'll show an error aggregation view — console groups related 500s by signature and shows top stack frames and affected routes. here's a cluster labeled 'decoder oom' — you can click into an example and launch a playground run with a smaller batch shape to repro.
[08:21] Tom: do we get symbols or stack traces from the runtime?
[08:24] Ethan: we surface high-level frames and kernel names; low-level native symbols are more sensitive and we treat them per-security policy but we can share obfuscated frames for debugging.
[08:35] Priya: if we do a POC, can we run the playback jobs in our VPC so traffic never leaves the environment?
[08:40] Maya: absolutely — for Private customers we offer an in-VPC control plane or an on-prem package. playback workers can execute inside your network and write artifacts to your S3.
[08:52] Sofia: any limitations on throughput for replaying large windows? we may want to replay a day's worth of requests for a thorough root-cause.
[08:59] Ethan: replays are horizontally scalable; limits depend on your Dedicated pool size. for heavy replays we recommend provisioning a short-lived Dedicated cluster or bursting to Hosted capacity with redaction if needed.

[09:14] [09:14] Maya: okay we're at the 30 minute mark, want to do a quick recap and assign next steps?
[09:20] Sofia: yes please. this was super useful, we want the replay results and the security docs.
[09:25] Maya: action items i'll send in a moment. ethan will run the three replays and attach console links and playback recordings. we'll also include a short cost/throughput sketch and recommended qprofile changes.
[09:36] Tom: once we see the replay results we can decide whether to run a quick pilot on Dedicated.
[09:40] Priya: timeline wise we'd like to kick a pilot next week if possible.
[09:44] Maya: we can do that — i'll propose a kickoff for the week of 2026-09-29.
[09:49] Sofia: sounds good.

[09:51] [09:51] (wrap up)
[09:52] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll send the notes and links. any final Qs?
[09:56] Tom: none here.
[09:58] Priya: nope.
[10:00] Sofia: thanks y'all.

End of transcript.

Notes / artifacts referenced: shared deck: https://redwood.ai/decks/console-trace-lab (placeholder), security whitepaper: https://redwood.ai/security/soc2-kms.pdf (placeholder), sample playback link(s) to be sent by Ethan.
